source: People believe an old debt past the statute of limitations is 'gone'; in fact the debt isn't erased, and acting on it can restart the clock.
card: Dwight, 50, in Ohio, USA, who got a call about an old debt and is sure it's legally dead because it's years old. Relieved and a little cavalier, he writes in offhand messages.
why_it_matters: He's trying to rebuild, and the idea that a chunk of old debt has simply vanished feels like a lifeline he doesn't want questioned.
facts: There is an old unpaid debt in the user's name
A collector recently contacted him about it
He believes the debt is past the statute of limitations and therefore 'gone'
not_yet: You have not checked your state's statute of limitations against the debt's last-activity date
You have not confirmed whether the debt still exists, can still be reported, or whether paying it could restart the clock
You have not contacted the collector, made a payment, or otherwise acted on the debt
anchor: A debt being past the statute of limitations doesn't mean it's 'gone' - the limitations period limits when a collector can successfully sue you, but the debt still exists, can still be reported, and a collector can still ask you to pay. And in many states, making a payment or even acknowledging the debt can restart the clock. So 'it's past the SOL, so it's erased' isn't right, and acting on that belief can backfire.
anchor_source: US CFPB (Ask CFPB on time-barred debt and statutes of limitations): a time-barred debt still exists and can be collected by means other than a lawsuit; a partial payment or written acknowledgement can restart the limitations period in many states.
false_position: My old debt is past the statute of limitations, so it's completely gone - I don't owe it and it can't affect me at all anymore.
evidence: He checks his state's statute of limitations against the debt's last-activity date: the period to sue has passed, but the debt is not erased, remains reportable, and a payment could restart the clock.
evidence_source: CFPB time-barred-debt guidance: expiry of the SOL bars suing to collect but does not cancel the debt; it can remain on a credit report and be pursued by other means, and paying or acknowledging it can revive the limitations period.
updated_position: The limitations period for suing has passed, but the debt still exists, can still appear on his credit report and be collected by non-lawsuit means, and making a payment could restart the clock - so it isn't 'gone', and he should be careful not to inadvertently revive it.

7.text: I actually looked into it. In my state the limitations period for this kind of debt has indeed passed based on when I last paid - so they can't successfully sue me. But the write-up also said the debt still exists, can still be on my credit report, they can still ask me to pay, and that if I make even a small payment it can restart the whole clock. So it's not 'gone' the way I thought.
